strengths: Well-motivated frequency decomposition approach with clear visualization demonstrating effective separation of moiré patterns into high-frequency textures and low-frequency color distortions

Strong experimental results achieving SOTA or near-SOTA performance on FHDMi and UHDM datasets with a compact model (6.065M parameters), significantly outperforming heavier methods in efficiency-performance trade-off
Excellent practical efficiency with only 2.49 TFLOPs for 4K image processing, making the method suitable for high-resolution and edge device deployment
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 3-6) systematically validating design choices and demonstrating component contributions
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 2's 3D/2D analysis and Figure 5's visual comparisons) that align quantitative results with qualitative observations
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: contributions are primarily architectural combinations of existing techniques (dilated convolution-based decomposition inspired by [37], standard dual-branch architecture, well-established channel attention) rather than fundamental innovations

Insufficient justification for frequency decomposition superiority: while Haar wavelets fail catastrophically (PSNR 13.32), the paper lacks rigorous analysis of why the proposed kernel-based decomposition works better and never specifies the decomposition level L

Critical scale-robustness claim lacks rigor: the assertion that low-frequency components achieve ~50dB reconstruction PSNR is mentioned casually with unspecified downsampling factors and decomposition levels, undermining a key design assumption

Dual-branch training strategy appears ad-hoc: while intuitive justifications are provided, quantitative validation is limited; different hyperparameters across datasets (crop sizes: 512 vs 768) lack principled justification; interpolation step for joint training suggests possible design issues

Marginal improvements from core proposed components: learnable FCT provides only 0.13 PSNR gain (25.26 vs 25.13), hierarchical fusion shows negligible difference (Table 6: 29.02 vs 28.99), and SA-CA module contribution is not clearly isolated

Limited evaluation scope: only two datasets tested (FHDMi, UHDM); no evaluation on TIP-2018 or LCDMoiré; no cross-dataset generalization analysis; comparisons with general restoration models in Table 2 mix methodologies (some with pre-trained checkpoints)

Incomplete technical clarity: decomposition level L never specified, hierarchical fusion rationale poorly explained, Figure 4's fusion strategy lacks detail, Spatial-Channel Projection design appears arbitrary without ablation or comparison to alternatives
Weak justification for two-stage training complexity: Table 4 shows only ~0.4 PSNR improvement over end-to-end training, and this is not compared against a capacity-matched end-to-end baseline
Missing failure case analysis, ablation on loss functions, statistical significance testing, and societal impact discussion
Reproducibility gaps: code availability shown as placeholder, missing specifications for decomposition level L, layer-wise dimensions, and exact resize ratios for low-frequency branch

strengths: Strong experimental results on FHDMi and UHDM with significant margins (e.g., 25.26 PSNR on FHDMi vs. 24.88 for ESDNet-L) achieved with a compact model (6.065M parameters, 2.49 TFLOPs for 4K processing).

Well-motivated frequency decomposition approach with clear visualization (Fig. 2) showing that moiré patterns concentrate in high-frequency components while color distortions appear in low-frequency components.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including comparisons with multiple baselines, detailed ablation studies (Tables 3-6), and cross-validation of design choices such as the crop/resize training strategy.

Principled dual-branch architecture design justified by demonstrating that low-frequency components withstand 10× downsampling with ~50dB reconstruction PSNR, validating the scale-robustness assumption.
Clear advantages demonstrated over Haar wavelet-based methods, with thorough analysis of why standard decomposition approaches (e.g., Haar) fail for moiré separation.
Efficient model design suitable for high-resolution and edge-device deployment, with computational efficiency competitive with or superior to larger baselines.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The frequency decomposition kernel is directly borrowed from [37]; the SA-CA module combines standard attention with existing RDDB blocks; the learnable FCT is essentially concatenation followed by transformer layers. Core components lack innovation.

Insufficient justification for key technical choices: No frequency-domain analysis (FFT spectra) explaining why the proposed kernel outperforms Haar; no ablation comparing two-stage vs. end-to-end training on the full framework; no theoretical explanation for low-frequency scale-robustness; loss weights (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.1) set arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis.

Unclear technical exposition: The learnable FCT's distinction from simple concatenation is poorly motivated (Eqs. 4-5); PostFusion is vaguely defined as 'an Nf layer transformer block' without specifics; decomposition levels L never explicitly specified; crop location selection during stage-2 training unexplained, hindering reproducibility.

Unfair experimental comparisons: Haar baseline uses 2-level decomposition while the proposed method uses presumably L=4 levels—unequal comparison; visual improvements in Fig. 5 are marginal; absence of user studies despite claiming perceptual quality superiority; comparison with general restoration models (OSEDiff, AdaIR, MoCE-IR) seems cherry-picked as they weren't optimized for demoiréing.

Missing critical analyses: No cross-dataset generalization (e.g., training on FHDMi, testing on UHDM); no failure case discussion; no sensitivity analysis for crop/resize ratios, decomposition levels, or loss weights; no statistical significance testing; grammatical errors and dense Figure 3 harm clarity.

Overclaimed contributions: 'State-of-the-art' on UHDM is misleading (second in PSNR at 22.22 vs. ESDNet-L's 22.42); 'compact model size' not contextualized against ESDNet (5.934M); no theoretical grounding for why the decomposition works beyond empirical results.

Reproducibility gaps: Redacted code URL; random seed unspecified; batch size of 2 unexplained; critical hyperparameters (L value) missing; crop location randomization strategy unclear (per-image? per-epoch? fixed?).

Insufficient ablations: No sensitivity study for loss weights λ₁, λ₂; no analysis of transformer layer count N; hierarchical fusion shows minimal gains (0.03 PSNR, Table 6) with questionable justification for inclusion; two-stage training not rigorously compared against simpler alternatives.

strengths: Well-motivated frequency decomposition strategy with clear visualization demonstrating that moiré patterns concentrate in high-frequency while color distortions appear in low-frequency components

Comprehensive experimental validation including comparisons against 8 demoiréing methods and 5 general restoration models, with strong results on FHDMi (PSNR 25.26, SSIM 0.8518) and competitive results on UHDM
Practical efficiency with only 6.065M parameters and 2.49 TFLOPS for 4K processing, significantly outperforming larger baselines while maintaining performance
Intelligent dual-branch training strategy (crop for high-frequency, resize for low-frequency) well-justified by frequency component properties and validated by ~6 dB PSNR improvement
Substantial empirical advantage over wavelet-based methods (25.26 vs 13.32 PSNR against Haar), demonstrating genuine superiority of the proposed decomposition
Extensive ablation studies validating each component's contribution and establishing the importance of the dual-branch approach
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Fig. 2) and sufficient implementation details for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty at the component level: the frequency decomposition kernel is adapted from existing work [37], and SA-CA combines standard modules (RDDB, channel attention, gated FFN). Ablations show minimal impact from some components (Table 6), questioning their necessity

Insufficient analysis of the learnable FCT module: marginal empirical improvements (0.13 PSNR/0.004 SSIM) over fixed variant, unclear what is being learned, and limited justification for the added complexity
Lack of theoretical grounding: why the specific kernel (Eq. 1) is optimal for moiré separation is not justified; the connection to diffusion priors is mentioned but unexplained
Limited generalization analysis: only tested on FHDMi and UHDM with no cross-dataset evaluation; second-best PSNR on UHDM (22.22 vs 22.42) suggests method may be specialized to these datasets
Incomplete justification of two-stage training: why separate pre-training of branches is necessary is not explored; Table 4 shows end-to-end fails but lacks mechanistic explanation
Missing ablations and analysis: no study of deep supervision necessity, sensitivity to hyperparameters, crop-to-inference translation, boundary effects, or failure modes
Presentation issues: informal language ('awesome benefits'), grammatical errors ('reals'), typos ('benifits'), redundancy between sections, and blank code repository URL
Architectural details under-specified: exact channel numbers and depth specifications for transformer layers only partially provided (N values), limiting reproducibility details

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear articulation of limitations in existing frequency-based demoisring methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, UHDMi) with extensive comparisons against state-of-the-art methods
Practical efficiency: achieves competitive performance with only 6.05M parameters, significantly smaller than competing methods, with reasonable 4K inference speed
Thoughtful asymmetric training strategy tailored to characteristics of high and low-frequency components with solid empirical validation
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-6) demonstrating the contribution of each proposed component
Clear presentation with effective visualizations illustrating frequency decomposition and comparative results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (frequency decomposition, learnable FCT, SA-CA) are adaptations of existing techniques; contributions feel incremental
Insufficient justification for key design choices: the anti-aliasing kernel (Eq. 1) appears arbitrary, and benefits of crop/resize training strategies are asserted rather than rigorously justified
Marginal performance improvements: ~2% gain over ESDNet-L on TIP2018, ranks 3rd on UHDM dataset; visual improvements in Fig. 6 are sometimes subtle without statistical significance testing
Insufficient analytical depth: missing failure case analysis, no visualization of learned frequency decomposition patterns, limited insight into why method works beyond intuition
Reproducibility concerns: ad-hoc hyperparameter selections (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.1, crop locations) lack principled justification; SA-CA module description is dense and unclear; code not yet available
Limited scope: restricted to still image demoisring; no exploration of video demoisring, cross-dataset generalization, or generalization to other artifact types
Unclear necessity of Transformer architecture: paper doesn't establish why Transformers are essential versus equivalent CNN architectures
Experimental fairness: different baseline methods use different backbones and training protocols; comparison lacks statistical rigor and detailed complexity analysis
